explanation: Bh5 retreats the attacked bishop and keeps a real edge (-157, good for Black). Bxh3 looks tempting -- grabbing a pawn on the way out -- but gxh3 just wins the bishop back for nothing, swinging the whole thing to +42.
Nh3+ forces gxh3, the only way to deal with the check, then Qg2 is mate -- the king has nowhere left to go. A classic knight-sac-to-clear-the-mating-square pattern.

bxc6 removes the bishop that just gave check and holds things close to level (-25). Blocking the check any other way lets White's bishop escape with real material -- Ke7 drops a rook to Bxb7, and Qd7 is even worse after Bxd7+.

Qb5 keeps fighting and limits the damage to +151 for White. In the real game, Qg5 was played instead -- chasing the kingside attack while the queenside stayed undefended -- and the position jumped to +490 once White's pieces got loose there.
f5 is a normal space-gaining push here (+61) -- Ng6 or h6 score about the same, so this is just sound development, not a position with one precise answer.

Qd7 holds a genuine edge for Black (-105, winning). In the real game, Qxb3 was played instead -- grabbing a pawn -- which let White's bishop take the hanging f5 pawn next and swung the game to +247, the start of the real collapse.

Bc8 drops the loose bishop back to block the queen's path down the 8th rank, holding things to a bad-but-fighting +656. In the real game, Kd7 was played instead, walking the king straight into Ne5+ and a forced march that made it +937.

Ng4+ forks the king and the bishop on e3 in one move -- check first, then the bishop's gone next. Rxf6+ looks tempting too but it's dramatically weaker (+2 instead of +252) since it gives up the fork for a much smaller gain.
b5 hits the rook on a4 and gives Black real chances (-448). In the real game, hxg4 was played instead -- grabbing a pawn -- and the position dropped to -62, giving back almost all of the advantage.

a4 just continues normal queenside expansion (+124) -- h3 or Bd2 score about the same here. Nothing sharp is happening in this position, consistent with this being the one game this session with no real mistakes anywhere in it.
Qe7 keeps the full advantage (+455), eyeing ...Bc5 next. In the real game this position is drawn from, Qc7 was played instead, giving back a big chunk of the edge (+196) for no real reason.

Bxd8 simply takes the rook that's sitting there for free, holding the position to +248 instead of letting White's attack run unopposed. In the real game, Nc7 was played instead, missing the free rook entirely and letting it climb to +762.

Rb6 defends the a6 pawn with the rook and keeps White's edge to a fighting +164. In the real game, b6 was played instead -- pushing the pawn rather than defending it with the rook -- and Qxa6 crashed through immediately after, the single costliest moment of the whole game at +924.

White has to deal with Black's d-pawn, one square from queening with threats. gxf4+ removes the attacking knight with check and defuses it; anything passive here (Kg1, f3) walks straight into a forced mate.

Nxe3 saves the attacked knight by counter-attacking the bishop, keeping a real edge (-195, good for Black). In the real game, Bxg4 was played instead, grabbing a pawn but leaving the knight on f5 to be captured next -- a piece given up for nothing, though the game was won anyway.
O-O-O tucks the king away and keeps things close to balanced (+59). Bc4 or c6 here would have scored about the same -- safety mattered more than finding one exact move.

Rg8+ is the rook on g2 moving with check -- which also clears the diagonal for your bishop on f1, so Bxh3 captures Black's queen next move. The check and the discovered line-opening happen in the same move, which is the whole point of the combination.

Bxc5 trades into a forced sequence (Nxc5 Qxe5 Re8 Qxc5) that nets real material by the end -- not one flashy shot, just the only line here that doesn't hand the initiative to Black's queen on a8 instead.
Bg4 develops naturally into a dead-equal position (+7) -- a6 or Bf5 score within a few centipawns of the same thing. Standard opening development, nothing to find here.
Rd5 keeps a real edge here (-108, good for Black) in a game that was still under control at this point -- the actual collapse came two moves later.
